node.label: Cynthia R. Comacchio
node.date_label: “Nations Are Built of Babies” (1993) · The Infinite Bonds of Family (1999) · The Dominion of Youth (2006)
node.description: In The Dominion of Youth (2006), Cynthia R. Comacchio argues that modern adolescence in Canada was made through changing social relations, scientific ideas and national aspirations. Institutions and adult expectations shaped this stage of life, while young people developed distinctive generational identities and cultures. “Nations Are Built of Babies” (1993) connects the medical regulation of motherhood to state intervention, class relations and national efficiency; The Infinite Bonds of Family (1999) explains family change through adaptation to economic disruption, war and depression. In a review excerpt reproduced by the publisher, Linda M. Ambrose credits Dominion with demonstrating that a distinct youth culture preceded the 1950s and 1960s. Sharon Anne Cook praises Infinite Bonds as a readable synthesis connecting family and national history, but criticizes the series’ absence of textual notes for making its historiographical positions difficult to follow. Comacchio’s own “The History of Us” (2000) evaluates the field’s demographic, feminist and labour approaches and argues for treating age as a category of historical analysis.
node.representative_figures_and_works: “Nations Are Built of Babies”: Saving Ontario’s Mothers and Children, 1900–1940 (1993); The Infinite Bonds of Family: Domesticity in Canada, 1850–1940 (1999); “The History of Us”: Social Science, History, and the Relations of Family in Canada (2000); The Dominion of Youth: Adolescence and the Making of Modern Canada, 1920 to 1950 (2006; paperback and electronic editions 2008).
node.scope_note: Selected passages of the 2000 essay read, not its complete 54 pages. Cook’s complete review of Infinite Bonds read; its issue year remains unverified. JSTOR supplies book metadata and displayed chapter openings only. Dominion’s description, contents, edition list and publisher-selected review excerpts read; full book and original Dominion reviews unread. Nations Are Built of Babies and the other historians’ monographs remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The History of Us” (2000), Comacchio uses Parr’s The Gender of Breadwinners (1990) to explain why women’s importance to family earnings did not necessarily give them equal household authority.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 199–200 and n. 59. Comacchio explains Parr’s challenge to ‘binary opposites’, follows the two Ontario towns, and develops the implications of the gap between women’s economic roles and their familial power. Named constructive reception within Comacchio’s argument; no supervision, collaboration, exclusive influence or reciprocal endorsement asserted. Parr’s book was not independently read.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The History of Us” (2000), Comacchio uses Sangster’s Earning Respect (1995) to connect remembered respectability with working-class women’s family identities and subordination.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read p. 189, paragraph beginning But, as Joan Sangster, with n. 41; also p. 188 n. 39. The substantive discussion praises Sangster’s critical handling of memory and uses her Peterborough study to explain how support networks could reproduce dependency. The phrase ‘neither entirely’ marks a qualified account of memory, not acceptance of recollection as transparent fact. Earning Respect and the separate 1994 oral-history essay remain unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Sangster’s oral histories as an analytical resource

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The History of Us” (2000), Comacchio draws on Strong-Boag’s The New Day Recalled (1988) to explain how interwar media tied women’s opportunities and identities to domestic roles.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 196–197, especially p. 197 and n. 55. Comacchio calls Strong-Boag’s and Andrée Lévesque’s books ‘path-breaking life-course studies’, then distinguishes Strong-Boag’s analysis of family magazines, homemaking and consumption. Credit is limited to the named book’s use in this synthesis; Lévesque retains her own credit. No shared institutional affiliation or broad personal influence is inferred. The 1988 book remains unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Strong-Boag’s life-course history in the family synthesis

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The History of Us” (2000), Comacchio uses Ariès’s childhood history (1960; English translation 1962) to frame age as historically variable alongside class, gender and race, while reporting criticism of its narrow social evidence.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 184–185, section ii opening and n. 34. Comacchio credits the international stimulus of Ariès’s book and adopts historical specificity as the premise for discussing age, while retaining the criticism of generalization from upper-class materials. The note distinguishes 1960 original publication from the cited 1962 English edition. This is bounded intellectual reception, not agreement with every Ariès thesis. Neither edition was read independently.
proposed_edges.map_label: Ariès’s historical childhood, with evidential limits

proposed_edges.relationship: The Dominion of Youth (2006) explains modern adolescence in Canada as a historical formation shaped by scientific ideas, national projects, institutions and young people’s changing relations with adults.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete publisher description and contents on WLU Press’s book page, with the 2006 original-year metadata retained in graph source cdnsrc_comacchio_2006 (also corroborated by an indexed journal bibliography whose PDF fetch failed); no full-book reading. Comacchio’s own 2000 essay, pp. 184–187 and 219, already argues for age as an analytical category. The publisher page lists 2008 paperback and electronic editions; these are not treated as the first publication. Existing field prose and roster already name Comacchio; this proposal adds a person-entry relationship, not a duplicate roster row.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The History of Us” (2000), Comacchio argues that demographic studies clarify family structures and economic adaptation but cannot by themselves reveal power, choices and relationships inside households.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read p. 184, concluding paragraph of section II.i, following the Katz, Gossage and Canadian Families Project discussions. She explicitly affirms demographic research before identifying what numerical data cannot establish about unequal family members. ‘very little’ refers specifically to internal power dynamics. The target is the quantitative approach within this umbrella, not every form of family history or a rejection of demographic evidence.
proposed_edges.map_label: Limits of demographic inference about household power

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The History of Us” (2000), Comacchio presents Nations Are Built of Babies (1993) as an analysis of scientific motherhood linking medical and state regulation of maternity to class and gender relations.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 186–187, first-person account beginning My own work, and n. 37. Comacchio names ‘social reproduction theory’ and explains her study’s relation to medical/state intervention, material constraints and national efficiency. The adjacent comparison with Katherine Arnup is credited separately. This establishes a specific contribution to women’s and gender history through the argument, not field membership inferred from subject or employer. The 1993 book remains unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Scientific motherhood, state policy and social reproduction

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Mechanomorphosis: Science, Management, and “Human Machinery” in Industrial Canada, 1900–45’ (1998), Comacchio contributed to Canadian working-class history by connecting scientific management and industrial health with attempts to regulate workers’ bodies; Eric Strikwerda subsequently uses this analysis in his study of industrial nutrition (2019).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Strikwerda’s journal-hosted HTML, especially the body discussion at the beginning of ‘Nutrition Science and the Industrial Body’ and its notes 15–17. This is substantive use: the body quotes Comacchio’s account of bodies and machines as components of industrial capitalism, and note 17 identifies pp. 41–42 of her 1998 article. Also read the original article’s opening pp. 35–38 and conclusion pp. 65–67 on the journal’s own PDF route. These passages connect labour discipline, medicine and bodily regulation, while the conclusion recognizes the limits of attempts to make workers function like machines. The edge records this specific contribution, not foundation of the field. Strikwerda is not an eligible person endpoint, so no person-to-person edge is proposed.
proposed_edges.map_label: Scientific management, industrial health and workers’ bodies
